walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: a key-press loop

steps.text: This is a different loop. The right arrow is checked 3 times: pressed, not pressed, pressed.
Check 1: the decision asks about the key. It is pressed, so follow True.
steps.visual: Check 1: pressed

steps.text: Point in direction 90: the sprite faces right.
steps.visual: Facing: 90 (right)

steps.text: Move 5 steps. Then the arrow goes back to the decision.

steps.text: Check 2: not pressed. Follow False. It goes straight back. No move.
steps.visual: Steps so far: 5

steps.text: Check 3: pressed. True: Point, then Move 5 steps. 5 + 5 = 10.
steps.visual: Steps so far: 10

steps.text: No more checks. 2 presses x 5 steps = 10 steps. Now count the presses in your question.
steps.visual: Altogether: 10 steps

steps.label: Key Words: AND, OR, NOT
steps.content:
Key Words: AND, OR, NOT

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a decision give 1 or 0?Show the answer

A decision has only two arrows. 1 follows True and 0 follows False.

1 means True. 0 means False. Example: Up is 1 (pressed), Right is 0 (not pressed).

WordRuleExample
AND1 only when both parts are 1.Up AND Right is 0.
OR1 when at least one part is 1.Up OR Right is 1.
NOTSwaps the value: 1 becomes 0, 0 becomes 1.NOT Up is 0.
Decision1 follows the True arrow. 0 follows the False arrow.0: follow False.

The same keys for both: Left is pressed (1). Down is not pressed (0).

Same: the same keys and the same boxes.

Different: one word. A uses AND: 1 AND 0 is 0, so A says Stand. B uses OR: 1 OR 0 is 1, so B says Slide.

steps.label: Comparing Numbers
steps.content:
Comparing Numbers

A decision can compare two numbers. The answer is 1 (True) or 0 (False).

  • > bigger than
  • < smaller than
  • = the same
  • <> not the same
Think → Pair → SharePredict: Score is 15. Target is 20. What does the sprite say?Show the worked answer

Put the numbers in: 15 > 20? Is 15 bigger than 20? No: 0.

0 follows the False arrow. The sprite says Try again.

Different: the sign. A: is 20 bigger than 20? No: 0, so A says Try again. B: is 20 the same as 20? Yes: 1, so B says Win.

steps.label: Sub-routines and CALL
steps.content:
Sub-routines and CALL

A sub-routine is a named part of an algorithm. It is written once, as its own flowchart.

  • CALL jumps to the sub-routine. It runs from its own Start.
  • At its End, Main carries on just after the CALL.
  • Written once, used many times.
Think → Pair → SharePredict: how many steps does the sprite move altogether? How many times is DrawSide written out?Show the worked answer

Each CALL runs DrawSide once: 40 + 40 = 80 steps.

DrawSide is written out once. It is CALLed twice.

steps.label: Your Turn: Follow the CALL
steps.content:
Your Turn: Follow the CALL

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is a sub-routine written only once?Show the answer

Each CALL runs the same flowchart again. We never copy its boxes.

Begin at Main's Start.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Compare: Two Mains, One Sub-routine
steps.content:
Compare: Two Mains, One Sub-routine

Main A and Main B both CALL the same sub-routine, Hop.

Think → Pair → ShareWhat is the same? What is different? How many steps does each sprite move?Show the answer

Same: both CALL Hop twice, so both say Hop, Hop.

Different: B has a Move box between the CALLs. A moves 10 + 10 = 20 steps. B moves 10 + 20 + 10 = 40 steps.
